Fully integrated perovskite active polaritonic circuits

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 47 min read (9464 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~47 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, photonic integrated circuits are emerging as a key technology for compact, analogue and energy-efficient optical information processing1.
  • Integrated photonic devices have emerged as a powerful platform for the next-generation information technologies, and the development of efficient and scalable integrated photonic circuits has become a central focus of state-of-the-art research.
  • According to recent reports, however, the effectiveness of all-optical devices depends critically on the ability to harness optical nonlinearities.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, photonic integrated circuits are emerging as a key technology for compact, analogue and energy-efficient optical information processing1. Yet, their practical implementation remains limited by the intrinsically weak optical nonlinearities of conventional materials, which demand high power and large device footprints to achieve substantial nonlinear responses2. Exciton–polaritons, hybrid light–matter excitations of semiconducting materials, offer a promising route to overcome these limitations by combining strong optical nonlinearities with the high speed and scalability typical of photonic platforms3,4,5. However, despite their potential, fully integrated on-chip polaritonic systems simultaneously delivering room-temperature waveguide lasing, controllable optical routing and amplification have remained elusive. Here we demonstrate a fully integrated perovskite polaritonic circuit that brings these functionalities together in a single-step-grown platform. We realize precise and scalable polariton circuits with integrated gratings that act as both couplers and reflectors, enabling in-plane Fabry–Pérot cavities. These structures support robust in-plane polariton lasing with coherent guided emission at a geometry-defined wavelength, optical amplification of propagating polaritons and nonlinear optical phase control exceeding π, all within the same on-chip architecture. Our results establish perovskite polariton circuits as a scalable platform for active and interferometric integrated photonics.

Integrated photonic devices have emerged as a powerful platform for the next-generation information technologies, and the development of efficient and scalable integrated photonic circuits has become a central focus of state-of-the-art research. Photonics enables ultrafast signal propagation, low-loss transport, broadband modulation and highly efficient information processing6,7. In this context, it is crucial that the same architecture supports a variety of integrated components, including on-chip coherent light sources, frequency-comb generators, modulators, amplifiers and switches, enabling coherent phase manipulation of propagating optical fields as a key functionality for dynamical reconfigurability and interferometric-based operations.

According to recent reports, however, the effectiveness of all-optical devices depends critically on the ability to harness optical nonlinearities. As conventional platforms based on linear dielectric materials or lithium niobate (LiNbO3) show intrinsically weak nonlinear responses8,9, structures supporting exciton–polaritons have been proposed as an effective alternative. These hybrid light–matter excitations, formed under non-perturbative radiation coupling between excitons and purely photonic eigenmodes, combine photon-like propagation with strong optical nonlinearities, making them attractive for ultrafast all-optical information processing10,11,12,13. Although exciton–polaritons have been extensively studied in vertically confined microcavities, planar architectures such as polariton waveguides14,15,16,17 have recently attracted increasing interest owing to their ability to confine light within smaller modal volumes, thereby enhancing exciton–photon coupling, increasing polariton group velocities and facilitating on-chip integration. When combined with suitable active materials showing large exciton binding energies, polariton operation can be sustained at room temperature5, a condition fulfilled by perovskites, which stand out for their exceptional and tunable optoelectronic properties and ease of processing, eliminating the demanding fabrication procedures typically required for conventional semiconductors. In addition, their strong polariton nonlinearities, comparable to that of gallium arsenide (GaAs)-based systems, makes them an increasingly attractive platform for polariton-based applications at room temperature18,19,20,21. However, fabricating high-quality perovskite photonic components remains challenging because well-defined edges and smooth surfaces are essential for achieving satisfactory performance22,23,24, whereas conventional postprocessing often degrades the crystal morphology and optical quality. Despite recent progress, efficient in-coupling and out-coupling of light remains a main bottleneck. In particular, the realization of coherent on-chip tunable light sources, optical amplification of propagating polariton signals and efficient nonlinear phase control—only partially explored in planar microcavities under cryogenic conditions25 and still absent in guided propagating polariton systems—remains a key outstanding challenge. Overcoming these limitations is crucial to achieving robust, room-temperature, scalable and fully integrated nonlinear photonic devices.

Here we address these critical challenges by developing a fully integrated perovskite-based polaritonic circuit in which waveguides and grating couplers are simultaneously defined within the active materials using an innovative bottom-up soft-lithographic strategy that combines surface-tension-assisted and microfluidic growth processes26,27,28. This growth approach eliminates the need for any subsequent postprocessing, enabling the direct integration of hundreds-of-micrometres-long, micrometre-wide caesium lead bromide (CsPbBr3) waveguides with subwavelength gratings featuring tunable periodicity and filling factors. Under off-resonant pumping, the integrated gratings provide longitudinal optical feedback, enabling polariton lasing in an in-plane Fabry–Pérot cavity, with emission efficiently propagating along the waveguide and readily tunable by means of the grating geometry. We also demonstrate efficient optical amplification in a two-beam experiment, in which a resonantly injected propagating polariton wavepacket is amplified through stimulation from the exciton reservoir created by an extra off-resonant beam. The threshold-like amplification resembles key features of spiking neurons, offering a promising route towards the development of neuromorphic polariton devices29,30. In parallel, we achieve nonlinear optical phase control of propagating polariton signals, enabling interferometric functionalities with phase shifts reaching 2π. Our results demonstrate room-temperature polaritonic circuits with active nonlinear functionalities, marking an important step towards ultra-compact, highly nonlinear polariton devices for integrated photonics and optical information processing.

CsPbBr3 perovskite waveguides with various geometries were directly fabricated on glass substrates using a modified soft-lithography approach that combines surface-tension-driven lithography with microfluidic processing from a liquid precursor solution, following the procedure sketched in Fig. 1a and detailed in the Methods (Supplementary Figs. 1–4). The process uses a patterned polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) replica moulded from a silicon master (Fig. 1b), yielding the perovskite waveguides with integrated gratings shown in Fig. 1c–e. This hybrid method enables the direct formation of hierarchical architectures through controlled self-assembly under saturation conditions and controlled temperature, yielding micrometre-scale waveguides decorated with integrated nanometric grating arrays. The soft-lithography route overcomes key limitations of conventional fabrication by exploiting elastomeric replication, enabling a simple, low-temperature and non-destructive process. It eliminates the need for multi-step lithography, avoids postprocessing damages and refractive-index mismatches, while significantly reducing fabrication cost and time.

a, Schematic illustration of the fabrication process of CsPbBr3 waveguides by means of microfluidic surface-tension-driven lithography. The process follows three main steps: (1) replica moulding in PDMS of the waveguide master (left); (2) capillary-driven distribution of the precursor solution along the microstructured channels under saturated conditions and controlled temperature (centre) and (3) formation of CsPbBr3 microcrystals with the desired morphology and integrated nanometric optical gratings (right). b, Scanning electron microscope (SEM) images of representative waveguides with integrated optical gratings fabricated on the silicon master through electron-beam lithography (EBL). c, Confocal images of CsPbBr3 perovskite waveguides with integrated gratings produced by the modified single-step soft-lithography technique described in a. Its features reproduce closely those fabricated in the master. d, SEM image showing a complete grating coupler directly replicated onto the CsPbBr3 perovskite structure. Right inset shows high-resolution view of the grating from the white region in the left panel. e, High-resolution atomic force microscopy (AFM) measurement of a representative grating. f, TE-pol momentum-space photoluminescence map from one of the waveguide gratings. Here β denotes the waveguide momentum, related to the measured outcoupled wavevector by β = k ± 2π/a, where a is the grating pitch. For this specific grating, the pitch was measured to be 240 nm. Two polariton modes (yellow solid lines) are visible and marked as LP0 and LP1, respectively. The two polariton modes arise from strong coupling between two photonic modes (TE0 and TE1, white dashed lines) and the excitonic resonance. Right panel, real-space photoluminescence image of the waveguide in which the emission from several adjacent gratings is visible; the pumping spot is outside from the image in the top part. LP, lower polariton; TE-pol, TE-polarized. Scale bars, 10 μm (b,c,f); 2 μm (d).

Industry observers note that to investigate the optical properties of the fabricated structures, we performed momentum-resolved photoluminescence and reflectivity measurements (Methods). The corresponding maps for both transverse-electric (TE) and transverse-magnetic (TM) polarizations and different pitches are shown in Supplementary Figs. 5–7. The momentum-resolved photoluminescence, obtained by spatially selecting the emission from one grating, is shown in Fig. 1f for TE polarization. Two strongly coupled modes are clearly visible (yellow solid lines), which we attribute to the fundamental (TE0) and first-order (TE1) lower polariton waveguide modes. Although the upper polariton branch is not visible31,32,33, the characteristic dispersion of the waveguide modes, which is approximated as linear in the weak coupling regime (white dashed lines), indicates an increasing bending approaching the exciton resonance, providing clear evidence of the strong radiation-matter coupling. Reflectivity and photoluminescence data were fitted using a two-coupled-oscillator model yielding Rabi splitting energies of Ω = 140 ± 10 meV for both the TE1 and TE0 modes (Supplementary Figs. 5 and 6), consistent with previous reports23,34. The presence of these two modes is compatible with a waveguide thickness ranging between 250 nm and 290 nm, as confirmed by finite-difference time-domain simulations presented in Extended Data Fig. 1 for different grating pitches. It is vital to note that the TE1 mode appears brighter because one of its electric-field maxima lies closer to the top surface of the waveguide, where the grating is patterned, resulting in more efficient coupling to free-space radiation and a larger momentum-space linewidth. The typical real-space photoluminescence emission is shown in the right part of Fig. 1f and the exciton/photon fraction for LPB1 is reported in Supplementary Fig. 8.

According to recent reports, in the absence of external optical resonators, lasing in perovskite microstructures can arise from optical feedback provided by sharp crystal facets acting as Fabry–Pérot cavities.23,24,35,36. In waveguide geometries, this feedback occurs predominantly in the transverse direction23, thus proving ineffective for photonic integrated circuits, which normally demand longitudinal propagation. Moreover, this lasing emission lacks spectral tunability, as it is governed by the intrinsic balance between optical gain and loss within the material. Alternative strategies based on isolated perovskite blocks evanescently coupled to active waveguides24 can promote in-plane propagation, but are limited by weak field overlap and inefficient coupling. Longitudinal polariton lasing assisted by integrated grating reflectors was demonstrated in a GaAs-based waveguide at cryogenic temperature17 and in gallium nitride (GaN)-based waveguide at room temperature37. However, in these systems the lasing mode remains confined within the reflective elements, without efficiently coupling into a propagating waveguide mode. By contrast, our approach integrates tunable lasing emission within a guided architecture, providing a direct route towards integrated polaritonic circuits. Moreover, it is achieved through a simple, scalable growth process yielding waveguides with embedded couplers, unlike the more complex fabrication required for GaAs or GaN platforms.

Industry observers note that to verify the formation of such a longitudinal optical feedback, the perovskite waveguide was off-resonantly pumped between two couplers. The real-space TE-polarized photoluminescence maps at excitation powers (P) below (left) and above (right) the lasing threshold (Pth) are shown in Fig. 2a. At low pumping power, the two outcouplers are barely visible, as only a relatively small portion of the emitted light is effectively coupled into the waveguide modes. By contrast, at high excitation power, a pronounced signal emerges from both outcouplers, suggesting that a longitudinal feedback is taking place. Notably, the lasing signal extracted from the grating disappears in TM polarization (Supplementary Fig. 9), confirming the polarization sensitivity of the feedback mechanism. To further investigate the onset and evolution of the lasing emission, we performed a real-space energy-resolved measurement and evaluated the emitted intensity (Extended Data Fig. 2) collected from one of the two outcouplers for the lasing signal (integrated between 2.31 eV and 2.32 eV), as shown in Fig. 2b. A clear threshold is observed at roughly Pth = 55 µJ cm−2, consistent with previous reports on similar perovskite materials19,35,38,39. The transition is accompanied by a clear linewidth narrowing as reported in the inset. The energy-resolved momentum-space maps are shown in Fig. 2c for the below-threshold (left panel) and above-threshold (right panel) regimes, and the corresponding kx–ky maps are reported in Supplementary Fig. 10.

a, Real-space image of a Fabry–Pérot in-plane cavity formed by two gratings (highlighted by the dashed squares); below threshold (left) the emission is dominated by exciton recombination under the pump spot, whereas above threshold (right) the lasing mechanism takes place and the emission from the two gratings is stronger than the photoluminescence not coupled to the guided mode. b, Emitted intensity integrated at the grating position from real-space energy-resolved measurements as a function of pumping fluence. Data points are obtained from three consecutive power-dependence measurements performed on the same structure as shown in blue, green and orange dots. The black points represent the average of the three power-dependence measurements. Dashed black lines are guides for the eye. The inset demonstrates the linewidth below (black line) and above threshold (red line) obtained from energy-resolved momentum-space measurements. c, Corresponding energy-resolved momentum-space emission below (left) and above threshold (right). The white dashed lines indicate the TE0 and TE1 polariton modes propagating downward (dashed lines) and upward (solid line). d, Lasing emission from three different cavities formed by couples of gratings having different pitches (270 nm, 260 nm and 250 nm, respectively); when the pitch is modified the energy of the lasing energy shifts. Scale bars, 5 μm.

Lasing occurs where longitudinal feedback selects a single mode due to the balance between gain and losses taking place at the reflectivity maximum induced by the grating, where losses are minimal. This point38,40 is slightly red-shifted and momentum-shifted with respect to the bandgap because finite-size and thickness variation in the grating profile cause new loss-favoured grating-to-waveguide backreflections15, as discussed in Supplementary Fig. 11. Lasing modes show a clear blueshift with increasing power, and more Fabry–Pérot modes emerge within the same spectral region (Extended Data Fig. 3). Notably, our configuration does not rely on large reflectivity or a strongly developed stop band; rather, a small but finite reflectivity is sufficient to enable cavity formation and mode selection, owing to the excellent gain properties of CsPbBr3. To demonstrate the spectral tunability of the lasing emission, we have tuned the periodicity within the integrated couplers by keeping their mutual distance constant. As shown in Fig. 2d, for three different grating geometries with pitches of 270 nm, 260 nm and 250 nm, a progressive blueshift is induced from roughly 2.28 eV to 2.315 eV. The below-threshold and above-threshold dispersions for all the measured gratings are reported in Extended Data Fig. 4. It is important to note that in the present device geometry, longitudinal feedback from the grating couplers coexist with transverse feedback from the waveguide edges. Above-threshold spatially resolved measurements confirm this coexistence, showing a roughly doubled mode spacing for edge emission, consistent with two cavity lengths of roughly 25 μm and 10 μm, respectively (Extended Data Fig. 5 and Supplementary Fig. 12). Efficient propagation of the lasing signal along the waveguide allows its collection from the first outcoupler next to the grating-pair cavity element (Extended Data Fig. 6). From these data, together with further resonant propagation measurements, we estimate propagation losses, outcoupler attenuation and optical gain (Supplementary Figs. 13 and 14).

In the following section we demonstrate another key functionality of our system: the optical amplification, which has not been previously achieved in similar polaritonic platforms at room temperature. This is essential for integrated photonic circuits as it compensates for propagation and coupling losses, thus enabling efficient on-chip light transport. We resonantly injected a pulsed beam (signal) through the input grating on the LPB1 mode and monitored the transmitted signal at the output located 25 µm away. A second pulsed beam (amplifier) was off-resonantly exciting the centre of the waveguide between two outcouplers where it generates an incoherent exciton population, as schematically shown in Fig. 3a. The signal beam was kept in the linear regime, thereby avoiding self-phase-modulation effects41 (Supplementary Fig. 15). We recorded the output intensity by scanning the time delay between the two pulses, keeping the signal with a constant intensity and changing the fluence of the amplifier. Figure 3b shows the collected intensity as a function of time delay for three different amplifier fluences, 3 μJ cm−2, 20 μJ cm−2 and 38 μJ cm−2, indicated by the blue, orange and green curves, respectively (Methods). At low pump fluences, the output signal remains unchanged, whereas at higher amplifier fluences it is strongly enhanced at 0 delay (Δt = 0 ps) and then decays within roughly 50 ps, demonstrating amplification once a sufficient particle density is reached. The decay follows a single-exponential fit with a characteristic time of 20.5 ± 1.2 ps, more than 1 order of magnitude shorter than the bare photoluminescence decay (Supplementary Fig. 16). To further explain the effect, power-dependent measurements at Δt = 0 ps were performed, as shown in Fig. 3c. Here the bottom panel represents the photoluminescence intensity generated by the off-resonant amplifier alone, which increases quadratically with pump fluence (Supplementary Fig. 17), whereas the top panel corresponds to the intensity measured in the presence of both the signal and the amplifier beams, showing clear amplification with a marked threshold-like behaviour. This trend confirms optical amplification and is consistent with stimulated emission, where the probe stimulates particles from the incoherent exciton reservoir created by the amplifier, possibly assisted by acoustic phonons, recently shown to play a key role in perovskites42. The amplification threshold is found to occur at roughly Pth,Amp = 10 μJ cm−2, that is, well below the lasing threshold.

a, Sketch of the integrated optical circuit used to measure polariton amplification: the off-resonant beam (amplifier) creates an exciton reservoir whereas the resonant beam (signal) excites a polariton state propagating along the waveguide. At the output grating the signal is amplified (amplified signal) thanks to stimulation from the exciton reservoir. Amplifier energy is Eamplifier = 2.58 eV in all the measurements. b, Collected intensity of the amplified signal as a function of time delay for three different amplifier fluences, 3 μJ cm−2, 20 μJ cm−2 and 38 μJ cm−2; black dashed line indicate the exponential fit. The signal energy is Esignal = 2.31 eV. A positive Δt corresponds to the case in which the signal arrives after the non-resonant pump, allowing amplification to take place while the reservoir is present. The decay time, 20.5 ± 1.2 ps, is the average of the exponential-fit values obtained at pump fluences of 20 μJ cm−2 and 38 μJ cm−2, which yield 22.1 ± 1.4 ps and 18.8 ± 0.9 ps, respectively. c, Power-dependent measurements at time delay 0 ps. Bottom: green dots represent the intensity of the amplifier alone; top, orange dots show the intensity of the amplified signal as a function of the amplifier fluence. The signal energy is Esignal = 2.26 eV. The horizontal error bars represent the power fluctuations of the amplifier, whereas the vertical error bars reflect the standard deviation derived from the signal evaluation across slightly different spectral regions, providing an estimate of the systematic uncertainty. d, Amplification factor as a function of the signal energy for two different amplifier fluences (P1 = 25 μJ cm−2 and P2 = 35 μJ cm−2) as indicated in c by the blue and red dashed lines. The amplification closely follows the photoluminescence spectral profile, increasing with the photoluminescence intensity. The photoluminescence spectrum, shown in arbitrary units, is included for qualitative comparison.

To test the spectral efficiency, we selected two amplifier fluences (P1 and P2, blue and red dashed vertical lines in Fig. 3c), both kept between the amplification and the lasing threshold, and scanned the signal energy, keeping its fluence constant. Figure 3d highlights the amplification factor as a function of the signal energy, defined as \(A=\frac{({S}_{{\rm{out}}}-{A}_{0})}{{S}_{0}}\), where Sout is the total output signal, and A0 and S0 are the independently measured amplifier and signal contributions, respectively. Clear amplification is observed over a broad energy range, with a superlinear dependence on signal energy and increasing spectral efficiency due to more efficient scattering and reduced group velocity, which enhances the interaction time with the reservoir. Crucially, amplification is observed even at energies well outside the narrow spectral region where lasing occurs (Supplementary Fig. 18) thus ruling out a cavity-mode feeding mechanism, which would instead be confined to the narrow spectral region defined by the lasing modes. In Supplementary Fig. 19, we present representative real-space maps of the signal, the amplifier and the amplified signal. Moreover, at the highest signal energy for which propagation is still sustained in the system the amplification factor approaches two orders of magnitude. Taking into account the spatial extension of the reservoir (Supplementary Fig. 18), we estimate the optical gain within a simple one-dimensional model as g = ln(A)/L, where A is the measured amplification factor and L is the effective interaction length, approximated by the amplifier full-width at half-maximum (13–15 µm). This yields values in the range of 5 × 102–3 × 103 cm−1 depending on the signal energy. Moreover, above the lasing threshold, the amplified signal saturates (Extended Data Fig. 7), consistent with reservoir depletion induced by the self-oscillating mode. Combining room-temperature operation with liquid-phase synthesis, our results represent a great advance over GaAs-based or ZnO-based platforms, which instead require cryogenic operation and demanding epitaxial growth16,43. In addition, the strong-coupling regime enables amplification through bosonic stimulation rather than population inversion, allowing operation at lower pump powers than conventional gain media.

We then exploit the complex geometries enabled by our fabrication approach to demonstrate nonlinear phase control in a guided polariton system. A resonant signal beam (Eres = 2.265 eV) is injected through the input grating, propagates along the structure and is subsequently split into the two arms of an interferometric Y-splitter. At the end of each arm, the waveguide edges act as outcouplers, allowing for the formation of an interference pattern in the momentum space, directly accessing the relative phase difference between the two arms. A non-resonant pulse is then introduced in only one arm of the Y-splitter. A schematic of the configuration is shown in Fig. 4a, and the reflectivity image of the Y-splitter termination and the corresponding outcoupled signal are shown in Fig. 4b. A representative momentum-space map recorded with only the propagating signal shows the expected interference pattern (Fig. 4c), whose origin is confirmed by selectively removing one output from the detection path (Supplementary Fig. 20). We then monitor the interference fringe shift as a function of the phase-shifter pulse energy at zero delay Δt = 0 ps between the optical shifter and the propagating signal beam. As shown in Fig. 4d, where the intensity profile along kx is plotted as a function of the optical-shifter fluence, a pronounced shift is generated. The phase shift, extracted from sinusoidal fits of the interferograms, reaches up to 2π with increasing pump pulse energy (Fig. 4e). As a consistency check, moving the phase-shifter beam to the opposite arm reverses the fringe shift direction (Extended Data Fig. 8), whereas amplification is observed only in the pumped arm (Supplementary Fig. 21). We model the experiment using two polaritonic waveguides described by the same light–matter coupled dispersion, with one incorporating a small shift of the exciton resonance, as described in the Methods. At fixed probe frequency, this shift produces a change in the polariton wavevector and the corresponding phase accumulated over the propagation length is reported in Fig. 4f as a function of the exciton resonance shift.

The ends of the two arms outcouple the propagating signal and behave as spatially separated coherent emitters, generating an interference pattern in momentum space that provides direct access to the relative phase. b, Real-space image of the Y-splitter termination (top) and the corresponding outcoupled signal (bottom) when only the resonant beam is present. c, Representative momentum-space map showing the interference pattern arising from coherent out-coupling of the two arms. d, Evolution of the interference fringes for increasing phase-shifter fluence. The direction of the fringe shift is highlighted by the black arrow. Bottom black profile represents the signal alone. The device footprint is roughly 20 μm2. e, Phase shift as a function of energy per pulse, showing a continuous increase reaching 2π. f, Calculated phase shift considering two polaritonic waveguides described by the same light–matter coupled dispersion, with one incorporating a small shift of the exciton resonance. Scale bars, 2 μm (b), 1.5 μm–1 (c).

According to recent reports, finally, after establishing the presence of a suitable π-phase shift in the Y-splitter geometry, we extend this functionality to a full Mach–Zehnder interferometer. The polariton mode is resonantly excited at 2.265 eV through the input grating, while the transmitted signal is collected at the output, with the phase shifter applied to one arm of the interferometer, as illustrated in Fig. 5a,b. The output intensity is extracted from a fixed spatial region at the grating outcoupler and is shown in Fig. 5c after background subtraction (Supplementary Fig. 22). As the phase-shifter energy increases, the signal evolves from a maximum to a minimum and then back to a maximum, demonstrating a full 2π response well reproduced by a sine-squared fit. Notably, this sizable phase shift is achieved within an ultra-compact guided footprint (roughly 20 µm2, Fig. 5b), compared with millimetre-scale lithium-niobate phase shifters44,45. The large modulation is enabled by the polaritonic nature of the guided mode that enhances the nonlinear response to the pump-induced reservoir. Beyond its compactness, the direct use of polaritonic nonlinearities, with a residual contribution from the excitonic reservoir due to the off-resonant excitation, offers a route towards ultrafast integrated circuitry compared with thermo-optic nonlinearities46,47,48.

The phase-shifter beam was pumping one arm of the interferometer. The images of the signal input, phase shifter and signal output regions were acquired separately and subsequently rescaled in intensity. c, Signal output as a function of the phase-shifter energy: black dots represent the experimental data, and the red line indicates the fitted curve. The data are collected at Δt = 0 ps, corresponding to temporal synchronization between the travelling signal beam and the phase-shifter beam at the phase-shifter spatial position. Scale bars, 10 μm.

In summary, we demonstrate a fully integrated perovskite polariton waveguide platform operating at room temperature, combining strong nonlinear propagation, tunable polariton lasing, optical amplification and nonlinear phase control within a single device. Our approach introduces a hybrid and high-throughput soft-lithography method that combines surface-tension–guided assembly with microfluidics, enabling single-step direct fabrication of active waveguides with integrated grating couplers. This provides a straightforward, cost-effective and scalable route for realizing self-assembled complex polaritonic architectures without the need for specialized vacuum equipment or epitaxial reactors. The developed architecture supports on-chip polariton lasing, with wavelength-selective emission enabled by longitudinal feedback from the integrated gratings and efficient propagation along the waveguide. Beyond lasing, we demonstrate room-temperature amplification of guided polariton signals by nearly two orders of magnitude. The threshold-like amplification and nonlinear response suggest potential for neuromorphic polariton devices, in which tailored excitation geometries and pulse sequences could enable neuron-like operations such as signal integration and threshold-triggered emission.

Furthermore, we demonstrate nonlinear phase control in a guided polariton configuration, achieving phase shifts exceeding π within an ultra-compact footprint. Crucially, we harness this capability in a fully integrated Mach–Zehnder interferometer, enabling direct conversion of phase modulation into intensity modulation. The ability to coherently control the phase of propagating signals, combined with intrinsic ultrafast polaritonic nonlinearities, establishes this platform as a promising route towards ultrafast on-chip interferometric devices. These features—combining room-temperature operation, material tunability, scalable and cost-effective fabrication, and rich nonlinear functionalities—establish perovskite polariton waveguides as a versatile and promising platform for next-generation integrated photonic and polaritonic technologies.

In a recent development, the grating and waveguide nanostructures and microstructures were fabricated on 25 × 25 mm Si(100) substrates using EBL (RAITH Voyager) followed by reactive ion etching. The grating pattern was defined using a 130-nm-thick poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA) electron-beam resist layer spin-coated onto the silicon substrate and exposed by EBL at a dose of 580 μC cm−2. The exposed resist was developed in a MIBK:IPA (1:3) solution. A 40-nm-thick chromium film, serving as an etch hard mask, was subsequently deposited by electron-beam evaporation, and the remaining resist was removed in acetone. The pattern was transferred for 50 nm into the silicon substrate using fluorine-based reactive ion etching (CF4, CHF3, O2, Ar). The chromium mask was then removed by wet chemical etching. An analogous process was used for the fabrication of the waveguide structures, with optimized parameters as follows: PMMA resist thickness of 360 nm, EBL exposure dose of 280 μC cm−2, chromium mask thickness of 60 nm and reactive ion etching etching depth of 250 nm. Following chromium mask removal, the silicon master was cleaned in a piranha solution for 15 min to eliminate any residual organic contamination. The final silicon master featured microwire waveguides and interferometer-like geometries with lateral dimensions from 2 µm to 30 µm, and a height of 250 nm. Each waveguide incorporated nanometre-scale grating arrays covering areas of roughly 10 × 10 µm2, with a height of 50 nm, pitches between 240 nm and 300 nm and varying filling factors, directly etched onto the surface. The aspect ratios (height/width) of the patterned structures, including both the waveguides and the gratings, ranged from approximately 0.01 to 0.60. The grating width was intentionally designed to be smaller than the waveguide width (Supplementary Figs. 3 and 4), so that the grating lines remain confined within the inner region of the waveguide and do not overlap with the waveguide borders in the etch mask, thereby avoiding local sidewall indentations during the two-step dry-etching process and preserving a more uniform waveguide geometry for crystal growth. For the interferometer, the structure includes a sequence of lateral modulations before the Y-splitter, efficiently redistributing the guided mode into the two branches (Supplementary Fig. 4).

Sources indicate that perovskite devices were fabricated using a modified soft-lithography approach that combined surface-tension-driven lithography with microfluidic processing of a liquid precursor solution, using PDMS replicas moulded from silicon masters with predefined multiscale geometries. A mixture of PDMS prepolymer and curing agent (10:1, Sylgard 184, Dow Corning) was cast onto the Si master and cured at 140 °C for 10 min. The polymerized PDMS layer was then carefully detached from the master before the use. A 0.42 M precursor solution was prepared by dissolving 106 mg of CsBr and 183.5 mg of PbBr2 (1:1 molar ratio) in 1.2 ml of dimethylsulfoxide. The mixture was stirred at 80 °C on a hotplate inside a nitrogen-filled glove box for 2 h, yielding a clear solution. Immediately before use, the precursor solution was diluted to concentrations in the range 0.05–0.1 M for the CsPbBr3 crystal growth. The precursor solution was deposited in contact with the patterned PDMS replica until the capillary pressure required for complete imbibition of the microstructures and nanostructures was reached. Once nucleation began, with the liquid meniscus pinned to the sidewalls of the nanoscale features, the PDMS replica was placed in conformal contact with a glass substrate to seal the microwire waveguides26,27. At this stage, capillary forces and surface interactions guided the solution through the microfluidic channels. Within the confined geometry, the reduced precursor volume and the progressively increasing concentration and viscosity gradients promoted perovskite nucleation through surface-tension-driven self-assembly precisely at the elastomer–air interface of each microstructure and nanostructure28,49,50,51. Crystallization inside the microchannels was optimized by imposing controlled temperature ramps (from 4 °C to room temperature) and by maintaining controlled vapour saturation and a pressure of 0.02 N cm−2 (refs. 52,53). After complete solvent evaporation, the PDMS replica was removed, yielding CsPbBr3 positive structures directly on the glass substrate that faithfully reproduced the microscale and nanoscale features of the original Si master. To assess fabrication reproducibility, we report in Supplementary Fig. 23 a set of nominally identical microwire arrays fabricated under the same conditions. The samples indicated a consistent optical response, with only minor detuning variations. It is notable to note that the grating width was intentionally designed to be smaller than the waveguide width, see Supplementary Figs. 3 and 4, to preserve continuous sidewalls in the elastomeric microchannels used for soft-lithography growth, ensuring uniform capillary filling and crystallization conditions while avoiding sidewall discontinuities that could introduce structural defects or make the crystal more fragile during replica peeling. The accessible limits of the proposed fabrication approach were determined by the fidelity of pattern transfer from the master mould to the elastomeric replica and subsequently to the perovskite crystal. On the basis of the aspect ratios demonstrated here (0.01–0.6), we anticipate that perovskite waveguides with thicknesses of roughly 100–150 nm and lateral dimensions of roughly 250–400 nm should be feasible. For periodic nanostructures, we note that some of the geometries investigated in this work (Supplementary Fig. 2) already contain lateral features as small as 50–80 nm, approaching the practical resolution limit of standard PDMS-based replication. Further reduction of the feature size would probably require optimization of the elastomeric replica itself.

Confocal images were acquired using a Zeiss LSM 980 confocal microscope in high-resolution mode (1,024 × 1,024 pixel). Samples were prepared on microscope slides and characterized using a 488-nm excitation laser and a main beam splitter (MBS 488/639-nm) with appropriate photomultiplier tube (PMT) and gallium arsenide phosphide (GaAsP) detectors. All samples were imaged at various magnifications using Strategy-Apochromat objectives of ×10 with a numerical aperture of NA = 0.45, ×20 NA = 0.8 and ×40 NA = 0.95. Three-dimensional images were obtained using the Z-stack scanning mode, which generated optical slices at various depths. Image analysis across different acquisition channels, tomographic reconstructions, spectral profiles and three-dimensional rendering were performed using the dedicated ZEN BLUE software.

AFM measurements were performed with a Dimension Icon (Bruker AXS) instrument, equipped with the Nanoscope V controller. Images were acquired in air, at room temperature, in Tapping Mode to protect the samples from damage. A rotated tapping etched silicon probe (Bruker) with a nominal radius of curvature R ≤ 8 nm was used. The morphology of the Si masters was investigated using a Sigma 300 (Zeiss) field emission SEM operated at an acceleration voltage of 5 kV and with an in-lens detector.

Recent findings suggest that all the optical measurements were performed by using microscope objectives at ×100 magnification and a numerical aperture of 0.9 (Zeiss) in a reflection configuration. The pumping lasers were taken from a pulsed source (Pharos, Light Conversion) with a tunable repetition rate and a pulse duration of <290 fs, which drove two computer-controlled optical parametric amplifier (OPA) stages (Orpheus OPA, Light Conversion). The OPA outputs were independently tunable in wavelength and, depending on the specific measurement (single-beam or double-beam excitation), were used either simultaneously or individually. In all the experiments, the repetition rate was set to 10 kHz. Energy-resolved momentum-space maps were collected by imaging the back focal plane of the objective onto the entrance of a spectrometer (Andor, Kymera 328i Spectrograph), equipped with three gratings (150 lines per mm, 300 lines per mm, 600 lines per mm) and coupled to a two-dimensional charge-coupled device (CCD camera, Andor, iStar 334T). For photoluminescence off the resonance pump, the laser was set to 480 nm and the emitted photoluminescence signal was filtered using an edgepass filter (Thorlabs, FELH0500) to suppress the residual excitation laser and isolate the emission. TE and TM polarizations were defined with the waveguide axis aligned to the entrance slits of the spectrometer, such that the electric field was parallel (TE) or perpendicular (TM) to the grating periodicity. The two polarizations were selectively monitored by using a half-wave plate (AHWP10M-600) and a linear polarizer (GTH10M-A) along the detection line. The laser pumping power was controlled by using a variable neutral-density wheel filter. For double-beam experiments, the two OPA outputs were temporally matched by using a delay line (Newport, M-ILS 150CC DC Servo Linear Stage). Reflectivity measurements shown in Supplementary Fig. 5 were performed by using a broadband white-light illumination in a reflection configuration, with a spot diameter of roughly 10 μm on the grating coupler. For the photoluminescence measurements shown in Supplementary Fig. 7, the waveguide was excited between two gratings whereas for Supplementary Fig. 6 the emission from a single grating was spatially selected. With reference to Fig. 3b, the temporal profiles were obtained by subtracting the residual photoluminescence signal generated by the amplifier alone, which remained constant across all temporal scans. The amplifier-only signal was collected separately using the same exposure time and then subtracted from the measurements in which both beams were simultaneously present. The same procedure was applied to the measurements in Fig. 4c,d, for which the signal obtained with the phase shifter alone was recorded under identical conditions and subtracted from the corresponding datasets. For the amplification measurements, Δt = 0 ps is defined as the relative amplifier-signal delay that maximizes the amplified signal intensity at the pumped region. This delay was experimentally optimized at each amplifier power, thereby inherently accounting for the relaxation dynamics leading to the population responsible for amplification and their possible dependence on the amplifier power.

Infinitely periodic dispersions have been calculated taking into account fully dispersive experimental literature values for the real and imaginary parts of the refractive index54. To quantitatively relate the measured phase difference to a microscopic excitonic energy shift, we consider two waveguides governed by the same light–matter coupled dispersion, with one of them subjected to a small blueshift of the exciton resonance. To relate to this experiment, this blueshift came from the interaction between the signal and the reservoir created by the non-resonant pump. The system was probed at a fixed frequency (ω), such that the effect of the perturbation would not change the frequency of the mode, but rather modify its propagation constant. The observable phase difference after a propagation length L therefore directly reflected the difference in wavevectors between the two configurations, (Δɸ = ΔkL). The parameter Ω corresponds to the Rabi splitting energy whereas ωx is the exciton resonance energy. Note that the first outcoupler next to the grating-pair cavity element is well visible confirming efficient and long-range propagation of the lasing mode along the waveguide. Liverpool Confidential: Latest on new deals for Virgil van Dijk and Alisson as European giants circle, how Reds are trying to turbocharge academy recruitment and Joshua Abe's comeback

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1248 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dailymail

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Published: 12:01 EST, 18 November 2026 | Updated: 12:03 EST, 18 November 2026.
  • European clubs are on red alert over the futures of Liverpool stars Virgil van Dijk and Alisson – despite both players being keen to extend their contracts at Anfield.
  • One source told me this week that AC Milan and other Italian clubs have been sniffing around Van Dijk for some time, with talks ongoing internally at those sides.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By LEWIS STEELE, FOOTBALL REPORTER.

Published: 12:01 EST, 18 November 2026 | Updated: 12:03 EST, 18 November 2026.

European clubs are on red alert over the futures of Liverpool stars Virgil van Dijk and Alisson – despite both players being keen to extend their contracts at Anfield.

One source told me this week that AC Milan and other Italian clubs have been sniffing around Van Dijk for some time, with talks ongoing internally at those sides. Milan owner Gerry Cardinale and influential adviser Zlatan Ibrahimovic are mentioned to be huge admirers of Van Dijk, who turns 36 next summer.

Italy was also a potential destination for Alisson last summer after Juventus held talks with his camp. At one point, Juve fancied their chances of signing him.

Both players will, as it stands, be able to negotiate a free transfer to overseas clubs from January 1, but both Alisson, 34, and Van Dijk, 35, want to stay at Anfield.

It puts the ball in the court of Julian Ward, Liverpool's sporting director, who must decide what to do next.

There had been a long-standing unwritten rule at owners Fenway Sports Group of never extending deals for those over the age of 30, but this was broken in the exceptional cases of Van Dijk and Mohamed Salah 18 months ago, after the pair led Liverpool to their 20th league title.

Liverpool goalkeeper Alisson is keen to stay at the club despite reported interest from his native Brazil.

Reds captain Virgil van Dijk (right) also wants to extend his contract at Liverpool – even though AC Milan are showing interest.

Despite both players wanting to stay on Merseyside, there is understandably a great deal of interest from around the world in taking them on, with local reports linking several Brazilian clubs to Alisson recently.

It has been revealed that van Dijk is a regular at Liverpool youth-team matches, which shows his love of the club but may also lead to suggestions the Dutchman will move into youth coaching when he does hang up his boots. He took the first-team squad to the Liverpool FC Museum recently to learn more about the club's history – further highlighting his passion for the Reds.

Interest from abroad only strengthens the hands of Alisson and Van Dijk, however, when it comes to their demands over the salary and duration of their upcoming deals.

Recent findings suggest that alexis Mac Allister is another with an uncertain future, though his father and agent Carlos is hoping to hold talks with Liverpool in the coming weeks. The Argentine's future is less of a pressing glitch for the Reds, though, given his deal runs until summer 2028.

Joe Gomez and Kostas Tsimikas are among the other players whose contracts are up in June next year.

In a recent development, it was around this time last year that the wheels started to fall off the Arne Slot machine. The Dutchman was eventually sacked and we have not heard much from him since. One question I am often asked is what is Slot up to – and why has he fallen off the face of the earth?

Well, I can reveal the former Reds boss is biding his time and enjoying holidays with loved ones, including several trips to Ibiza. Slot and his son Joep have also visited South America, taking in games in Argentina and Brazil.

In a recent development, slot, who has also been attending matches at home, turned down the Netherlands national team job and a lucrative gig in Saudi Arabia. He also rejected approaches in the summer from clubs including AC Milan, who eventually plumped for former Manchester United boss Ruben Amorim.

In a recent development, he is waiting for the right opportunity and does not believe his stock has fallen in the same way, for example, as several axed United or Chelsea bosses. After all, Slot won the Premier League title and would be a fine hire for most clubs around Europe.

Former Liverpool boss Arne Slot (centre, bottom row) watches the Dutch Eredivisie match between Heerenveen and his old club Feyenoord earlier this month.

Slot is waiting for the right job to come up – emboldened by the knowledge he is a Premier League winner.

…but AI report makes grim reading for Arne.

A couple of interesting bits to pick out from the fantastic Global State of Football report by PLAIER, a firm spearheading the use of artificial intelligence in football.

Liverpool finished bottom of the table last season in PLAIER’s ranking of every team's coaches based on resources and how they performed – Regis Le Bris at Sunderland was top.

The Reds were in the bottom three for coaching efficiency, suggesting that squad quality alone is no guarantee of success. For a more in-depth look at the report, click here.

Reds hunt for academy recruitment guru.

Liverpool are in the process of hiring an academy ‘talent ID lead’ to help with their youth recruitment.

It has been revealed that regular readers of this column will know this area is a key metric Anfield chiefs measure success by. They are now hiring someone responsible for leading the identification and recruitment of academy talent between the ages of 13 and 18 across the UK and Ireland.

Notable recent arrivals from other academies at this age include current first-teamers Rio Ngumoha, Conor Bradley, Trey Nyoni and James McConnell.

Kop Kids: Amazing Abe lights up England duty.

Confidential readers will recall I revealed on October 15 that Joshua Abe was ahead of schedule in his recovery from a shoulder injury and set for just another month on the sidelines. And Abe was indeed on the pitch representing England Under 17s exactly a month later, scoring against Montenegro and then again against Poland on Saturday.

In the last 12 months, the 16-year-old has 14 goals and four assists in just over 1,200 minutes played. Those are phenomenal numbers and it would not be a surprise to see the winger back in the first-team training group again soon.

Joshua Abe has recovered from a shoulder injury and was back in action for England Under 17s this week.

Fancy running the line, Andoni?

Industry observers note that in the last break, the boss was spotted at the women’s Merseyside Derby. Now, he has been pictured at a local Sunday League match, taking pictures with youngsters who could not believe their luck.

These may seem like small gestures but they are a helpful way of winning hearts and minds among a fanbase whose pleas for Slot to take an active interest in all aspects of the club sometimes fell on deaf ears.

Manchester United are in town on Sunday, in case you needed reminding.

Since winning the Premier League title last year, Liverpool’s league record against the 'Big Six' is played 12, won two, drawn three, lost seven. That must improve, starting on Sunday, and there can be no excuses around a upcoming-manager bounce for Mauricio Pochettino - who will barely have had time to find his parking space at Carrington by the time he comes to Anfield.

According to recent reports, liverpool need to see more from their big-money signings Alexander Isak and Florian Wirtz, who have been excellent for most of the season but poor in some high-profile fixtures, such as the home defeats by Manchester City and Arsenal. Across his 19 games against Liverpool, Pochettino has only won three matches, drawing five and losing 11.

Don't forget, African sensation is joining Liverpool, deal is already agreed

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A deal has already been agreed for an African sensation who people should not forget about.
  • Giants are born and giants are toppled.
  • There was a golden era in the 1970s and 1980s, followed by bleak and dark times, succeeded by even darker times on the pitch barring one miracle night in Istanbul.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A deal has already been agreed for an African sensation who people should not forget about.

Football comes in waves. It ebbs and flows. From one generation to another. Giants are born and giants are toppled. A club like Liverpool has ebbed and flowed a lot more than others over the years.

There was a golden era in the 1970s and 1980s, followed by bleak and dark times, succeeded by even darker times on the pitch barring one miracle night in Istanbul.

It has been revealed that then along game the beacon of hope. Jurgen Klopp restored the faith at the club and took Liverpool back to the apex of the footballing world.

Now it's Andoni Iraola's job to sort out the mess he inherited from Arne Slot and follow in the footsteps of Klopp.

What Julian Ward is planning to make Liverpool the best team in the worldOf course, it's never just the head-coach who is responsible, especially these days in modern football. There's an entire operation behind Iraola. Ward sits at the helm as the club's sporting director and he has a vision to help Liverpool get back to the pinnacle. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Ben Knapton | 20 Nov 2026 20:00, Last updated: 20 Nov 2026 20:00.

In a recent development, coventry City vs. Crystal Palace is the sort of match that will keep Frank Lampard's men in the Premier League if they can prevail, an ex-Sky Blues striker has told Sports Mole.

Coventry host Crystal Palace in the Eagles' first fixture under new head coach Thomas Frank, who takes over from Pierre Sage with the Eagles languishing at the bottom of the Premier League table.

The hosts, meanwhile, are three places and two points better off in the relative safety of 17th spot, having taken nine points from their opening 10 games of their first top-flight season in 25 years.

Two of Coventry's three league triumphs this season have come at the CBS Arena, both against bottom-half rivals in Newcastle United and Sunderland, although Fulham and Hull City have also got the better of them in front of their own fans.

Former Coventry striker Mark Hateley - who scored 27 goals in a century of appearances for the Sky Blues - is fearing a new manager bounce for Palace, but warned his old club that this type of match could dictate their survival chances.

“You always get that bounce from a fresh manager," Hateley said. "You get it for one, two, three games, and then it starts to wear off. Thomas Frank is a proven tactician who sees things very swiftly within a team.

“Palace still have a really decent side with decent players, so I think he'll be in and about it quickly, and you'll see a style of play that he gets from what he sees in that group of players. Whether it lasts all the way through, I don't know, but I think he'll fix Palace into a side that will be OK.

According to recent reports, “Coventry are the other side. They've got to survive this year and build for the next two years: survival, survival, survival. Palace will know how to do it; they've got good enough players. But these are the games Coventry should be looking to win. These are the games that keep you in the league.”.

Saturday's match will mark the first meeting between Coventry and Crystal Palace since the 2011-12 Championship season, when the Sky Blues lost 2-1 away before holding the Eagles to a 1-1 draw at home.

Coventry earned their most recent victory against Crystal Palace shortly beforehand, prevailing 2-1 in February 2011 thanks to goals from Richard Wood and Marlon King.

Taking data across all competitions from Lampard's Coventry tenure so far and Frank's lengthy spell at Brentford from 2018 to 2025, the statistics somewhat favour the Chelsea legend.

Indeed, Lampard boasts more points per game, more goals scored per match and fewer goals conceded per match, while also winning one trophy in the form of the Championship.

However, those numbers must certainly be taken with a pinch of salt given Frank's substantially longer spell at Brentford, and the Dane's four full seasons in the top flight after winning promotion with the Bees.

Lampard's Coventry have nevertheless shown promising signs after he also succeeded in keeping Everton afloat in the top flight, though, so Saturday's edition of Frank vs. Frank is a challenging one to call.

Mark Hateley was speaking to Sports Mole on behalf of London.bet.

Both Racing de Santander and Real Sociedad will be aiming to make it back-to-back wins in Spain's top flight when they lock horns on Sunday afternoon.

Real Sociedad lead the overall head-to-head record between the two sides 49 wins to 34, while the Basque outfit have triumphed in the last three meetings.

Racing have a record of four wins, two draws and six defeats from their 12 league matches this season, with 14 points leaving them in 10th spot in the La Liga table.

Jose Alberto's side entered the November international break off the back of a 2-1 victory over Malaga, and they have actually won three of their last four games in all competitions.

The Green and Whites are the reigning Segunda Division champions, securing a return to this level courtesy of their excellent second-tier campaign in 2025-26, and their main aim for this season will be to consolidate back in the top flight.

Racing have not managed to overcome Real Sociedad since March 2011, while they have just one victory over the Basque side since January 2007.

The Green and Whites have been impressive on home soil this season, picking up 11 points from their six matches in front of their own supporters.

Real Sociedad, meanwhile, boast a record of seven wins, one draw and four defeats from their 12 league matches this season, with 22 points leaving them fifth in the table.

The Basque outfit are only four points off fourth-placed Real Betis, and an excellent run of form in Spain's top flight has seen them win five of their last six matches.

La Real are also playing in the Europa League this season, picking up five points from their four matches to sit down in 20th position in the league stage.

Real Sociedad's last league match ended in a 1-0 win over Rayo Vallecano before the November international break, and they will have their eyes on another three points here before heading to England next week to tackle Crystal Palace in the Europa League.

As for Real Sociedad, Alvaro Odriozola remains unavailable for selection due to a knee injury, while Ander Barrenetxea is a major doubt due to a hamstring injury.

Mikel Oyarzabal missed the team's final match ahead of the November international break through illness, but the attacker has since returned for Spain, and it is possible that he could start in a wide area on Sunday due to the form of Orri Oskarsson.

The 22-year-old, who is being linked with a move to Manchester United, has scored four times in 10 league appearances this season, including the winner against Rayo Vallecano last time out, and he is again set to feature in the XI.

Exor pays in €60m of Juventus’ €250m raise, but UEFA deal limits January prepares

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (467 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Juvefc

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Juventus shareholders have cleared a capital increase of up to €250m, and majority owner Exor has already committed €60m of it.
  • Juventus shareholders gave the board the power to raise up to €250m in new capital at the Allianz Stadium on 3 November.
  • In a recent development, part of the money is already committed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Juventus shareholders have cleared a capital increase of up to €250m, and majority owner Exor has already committed €60m of it. Giovanni Carnevali warned that the UEFA settlement means nothing extraordinary should be expected in January.

Juventus shareholders gave the board the power to raise up to €250m in new capital at the Allianz Stadium on 3 November. The vote came in the extraordinary part of the meeting and passed with 99.9% in favour. The same assembly approved the 2025/26 accounts.

In a recent development, part of the money is already committed. Exor has already paid in €60m as an advance towards the capital increase. That payment supports the club’s equity and finances until the board uses its upcoming authority. The majority owner has also guaranteed its own 65.4% stake in the raise and any shares other investors leave untaken.

The squad will not see the full sum. Shoring up the club’s finances across this season and next will take 45–50% of whatever is raised, according to Football Italia. That leaves roughly €100m mainly for first-team signings before the January window. Beyond keeping equity at a suitable level, the rest will go on controlling debt and keeping the team competitive, including transfers, Corriere dello Sport reports.

The accounts show why the balance sheet needs support. The consolidated loss for 2025/26 was €66.0m. That was €7.9m bigger than the previous year’s €58.1m. The result was in line with the forecasts in the club’s half-year report to 31 December 2025. The board had approved the accounts on 29 September. Another loss is expected in 2026/27, mainly because Juventus are in the Europa League rather than the Champions League.

It has been revealed that the assembly was Giovanni Carnevali’s first as chief executive. He promised a serious approach to the January window. His warning was just as clear. As a serious company, Juventus must honour its settlement agreement with UEFA and does not expect to do anything extraordinary.

That agreement was declared on 30 June. It is a three-year settlement with the First Chamber of UEFA’s Club Financial Control Body. It relates to Juventus breaking UEFA’s Football Earnings Rule over the three seasons from 2022/23 to 2024/25.

For supporters, the message is mixed. The capital increase gives the club fresh resources. The settlement still dictates how quickly that money can be used on the pitch.

Shareholders also criticised the club for keeping a low profile in recent years. President Gianluca Ferrero declared Juventus open to dialogue with Tether.

Sources indicate that the terms of the UEFA deal leave little margin. Missing the targets agreed with UEFA for the current season or the next two can lead to limits on the club’s UEFA List A and further sporting sanctions. The settlement runs until the 2027/28 financial year.

Everton could look to make a major statement in the January transfer window as David Moyes considers ways to strengthen his side’s attacking options.

After concerns over the team’s lack of goals, the Toffees are reportedly exploring a move for a forward with proven Premier League experience.

Manchester United’s Marcus Rashford has emerged as a potential target, with reports suggesting Everton are discussing the possibility of bringing the England international to Merseyside.

A deal would give Moyes another versatile attacking option, although several key details would need to be resolved before a transfer could progress.

According to Football Insider, former Everton chief executive Keith Wyness believes a move for Rashford is being discussed seriously ahead of the January window.

According to recent reports, speaking on Football Insider’s Inside Track podcast, Wyness stated: “Yes, this is definitely being talked about and quite strongly. And I think that could be an interesting solution.”.

The former Everton chief executive also pointed to Rashford’s previous loan spells and suggested that a move closer to Manchester could benefit the player.

“Rashford did well when he was on loan at Villa and at Barcelona as well. I think it could work, and I think being close to where he is in Manchester, just along the M63, could also benefit him greatly as well,” Wyness explained.

The comments suggest that a January switch is a possibility worth monitoring, although neither club has confirmed an agreement. Separate reporting from FootballTransfers has also indicated that Everton and Manchester United have held early discussions over a potential winter move.

Wyness drew comparisons with Jack Grealish, who has made an impact at Everton when available, adding: “We’ve seen Jack (Grealish) moving across that way as well, and when he’s fit, Jack is certainly a big asset for Everton. So I think Rashford would be a very interesting signing, and I’m hearing there’s a lot of smoke here; it’s definitely being discussed.”.

He then added: “I wouldn’t be surprised to see something happening in January.”.

Sources indicate that for Everton, Rashford’s versatility could be a major attraction. Although he has often operated from the left, he can also play centrally, potentially giving Moyes additional options across the frontline. His arrival could provide support for Thierno Barry and help address the team’s need for more goals.

However, the financial structure of any deal would be important. Everton would need to consider Rashford’s wages, Manchester United’s valuation and whether a permanent transfer or loan arrangement would be realistic. The forward’s willingness to join another Premier League club would also be a significant factor.

Sources indicate that rashford could represent an ambitious addition for Everton if the club can find an agreement that works financially. His Premier League experience and ability to operate in several attacking positions would give Moyes greater flexibility, while a change of environment could offer the player a fresh start.

The comparison with Grealish is particularly relevant to Everton’s approach. The club could look to provide Rashford with an environment in which he can rebuild his confidence and contribute more consistently, although any potential success would depend on his fitness, form and role within the team.

Nevertheless, a transfer is far from guaranteed. The reported discussions remain at an early stage, and Everton must still resolve the financial details and establish whether Rashford would be open to the move.

For now, Wyness’s comments add weight to speculation surrounding Everton’s January looks. If negotiations progress, Rashford could become a name to watch as Moyes looks to strengthen his attacking options for the second half of the season.

Leicester City have axed a partnership with BC.GAME, after the gambling shirt sponsor appointed 'international porn star' Eva Elfie as its latest ambassador.

Leicester confirmed fans who have purchased a replica shirt featuring the sponsor's name within the last 28 days can return it for a full refund or exchange by December 2.

Elfie, who has 4.8million Instagram followers, is known in Esports and gaming communities too.

In recent years, Leicester’s spectacular decline on the pitch has mirrored the relationship with their supporters.

During the years immediately before and after their stunning Premier League triumph in 2016, it was difficult to find a club more in tune with the fanbase.

But a series of baffling decisions – including the tie-up with BC.GAME – eroded trust between the club and their supporters.

Leicester are now in League One and face a long road back but sensible moves like this one suggest they are at least facing in the right direction again.

  • A struggling Sparta Rotterdam outfit will set out in search of a return to winning ways in Sunday’s Eredivisie clash against AZ Alkmaar at Het Kasteel.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Adepoju Marvellous | 20 Nov 2026 20:54, Last updated: 20 Nov 2026 20:58.

A struggling Sparta Rotterdam outfit will set out in search of a return to winning ways in Sunday’s Eredivisie clash against AZ Alkmaar at Het Kasteel.

The visitors, meanwhile, travel to Rotterdam aiming for back-to-back wins for the first time since September, having snapped a three-game losing streak just before the international break.

AZ Alkmaar started the season with six wins and a draw from their opening seven Eredivisie matches, looking like the team to beat, but a 2-0 defeat to Feyenoord after the September break sparked a four-game winless run (D1, L3).

In arguably the game of the season so far, Leeroy Echteld’s men scored three times in the final 30 minutes of their most recent clash against Groningen to secure a 4-3 victory and keep themselves within three points of PSV Eindhoven at the top of the Eredivisie table.

De Kaasboeren have failed to win any of their league matches immediately preceding a Europa League group-stage fixture so far, and with a trip to Sparta Prague to follow this weekend, they will be eager to buck that trend of faltering domestically before continental duties.

AZ won both league meetings with Sparta last season, making it four wins from the last six encounters (D1, L1). Sunday’s visitors are also unbeaten in their last six trips to Het Kasteel, averaging two goals per game in that stretch.

However, AZ have struggled away from home recently, collecting just one point from the last nine available on their travels, which came in a 2-2 draw at Cambuur courtesy of a Mexx Merdink penalty seven minutes from time.

While not their heaviest, Sparta’s 3-1 defeat to newly-promoted ADO Den Haag was arguably their most disappointing loss of the 2026-27 season so far, especially given the momentum they carried into the clash after a thrilling 3-2 triumph over Groningen.

Rogier Meijer has now lost more than half of his 13 matches since taking charge in July, and pressure is beginning to mount on the 45-year-old.

Nevertheless, his experience at this level - having recently surpassed 200 matches as a manager in Dutch football - suggests he will be given time to turn things around.

Starting this weekend’s clash just two points clear of the drop zone, De Rood-Witte Gladiatoren risk ending matchday 13 inside the relegation places - a significant fall from grace for a side tipped to compete for Europe at the start of the campaign.

Only Utrecht and Willem II have conceded more goals than Sparta’s 29, and they are also one of five teams without a clean sheet, leaving little mystery about their biggest shortcoming this season.

Averaging 1.8 goals per game so far, Sunday’s hosts have fared reasonably well in attack, but an overreliance on Milan Zonneveld, who has been directly involved in nine of their 21 goals, can sometimes prove detrimental.

Sparta Rotterdam Eredivisie form:.

Sparta Rotterdam form (all competitions):.

AZ Alkmaar form (all competitions):.

Goalkeeper Michael Brouwer is Sparta’s only injury concern for Sunday’s clash after he was forced off late in the defeat to ADO Den Haag.

Filip Bednarek replaced Brouwer off the bench last time out and is ready to deputise in goal again if required.

Lushendry Martes will need to keep his discipline in check, having already collected four yellow cards this season, as one more would trigger a one-match suspension.

Jizz Hornkamp has made just three appearances this season and remains unavailable for AZ, as do fellow Dutchmen Stije Resink and Jeroen Zoet, who are both yet to feature in 2026-27.

Lewis Schouten’s involvement this weekend is currently in doubt after he was absent from the win over Groningen.

Twenty-three-year-old Mexx Meerdink has six goals and an assist in his last seven club matches and will be expected to deliver once again.

Sparta Rotterdam possible starting lineup:.

Bednarek; Martes, Young, Verschuren, Martins Indi, Kuipers; Van Bergen, Quintero, Hatenboer, Babadi; Zonneveld.

AZ Alkmaar possible starting lineup:.

De Busser; Chavez, Hoedt, Goes, Dijkstra; Koopmeiners, Kwakman; Daal, Byskov, Oufkir; Meerdink.

While Sparta’s defensive issues need no introduction, AZ have also struggled at the back recently, so a clean sheet for either side seems unlikely.

That said, Echteld’s men are strong favourites to get the job done, and we expect them to do so with relative ease.

The trip to Alkmaar returned Teun Koopmeiners to his former club. His brother Peer was in the AZ side that Juventus then held off. UEFA picked out the family meeting in its matchday 4 round-up.

Koopmeiners opened the scoring in the 19th minute from a Kolo Muani pass. Kolo Muani doubled the lead in the 37th minute, with Nick Woltemade credited with the assist, and Juventus led 2-0 at half-time. Kolo Muani earned a rating of 8.61 from the data provider, with Koopmeiners on 8.2.

According to recent reports, AZ pulled one back in the 88th minute. Mexx Meerdink scored from an Elijah Dijkstra assist. The hosts could not find an equaliser in the remaining minutes.

Recent findings suggest that the home side had 56% of possession. They completed 523 passes to Juventus’s 378. Eleven of AZ’s attempts were blocked, against three of Juventus’s.

Sources indicate that both teams put three shots on target. Vicario made two saves for Juventus. AZ’s expected goals total points to the chances the hosts created without converting them.

The figures are consistent with a Juventus side defending a first-half lead. Spalletti’s team committed 20 fouls to AZ’s 13. Andrea Cambiaso, Jeff Ekhator and Juan Cabal were booked for Juventus. Wesley Hoedt was the only AZ player shown a yellow card. Damian Sylwestrzak refereed the match.

Sources indicate that the victory was Spalletti’s second in a row in all competitions, following the league win over Napoli. It came after a run that included a 0-2 defeat to Genoa and a 0-3 loss to Lazio. Koopmeiners now has four goals for Juventus in all competitions in 2026, one more than the three he scored for the club in 2025, Sky Sport Italia noted.

For AZ, the result was a third straight defeat in all competitions. Losses to Ajax and Twente came before Thursday’s game.

This season’s league phase has 36 clubs, and each plays eight different opponents. It ends on Thursday 28 January 2027. Juventus host Omonia Nicosia on 26 November at 21:00 CET, while AZ travel to Sparta Praha. Juventus then visit Hapoel Beer-Sheva on 10 December and Ferencváros on 21 January 2027, both at 18:45 CET. They finish at home to Real Sociedad on 28 January 2027 at 21:00 CET.
